name: Kira Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights at the chilled-food warehouse out on the Eastbrook ring road. We supply about 140 supermarkets, so it's yoghurt, cheese, ready meals, all at three degrees. I lead a team of 14 pickers, and I still pick myself because I'm faster than most: a headset tells me the aisle and the slot, I say the check number back, and I build the pallet. The cold gets into your knees by four in the morning, but I like my crew and I like a clean, square pallet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The rate wears me out. The system counts my cases per hour and so does my manager, and a bad night means a talk in the office. What keeps me there is the people, honestly, and that there's not much else round here that pays even this badly. Jonas, my partner, works part-time at a bike shop, and we've got less than a month's rent put by, so I can't exactly walk out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now maybe the bosses will stop waving robots at us every time we ask for a pay rise. At work I'd tell the crew this is our chance to push for recognition of the union, because nobody can say we'll all be replaced next year. Online I'd probably share something about pay, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job stays, but my money problem stays too. The rent on our flat went up 60 a month in the spring, and Jonas's hours got cut at the bike shop. So nothing changing isn't the same as things being fine for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my nights and keep pushing the union drive, because that's the one thing that might change my pay. I'd try to put 50 a month aside, even if it's the bus instead of the car some weeks. I wouldn't go near any AI stuff; I don't need it to pick yoghurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's the same grind, and the grind already has me checking my bank app before I buy a coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the union drive is the one thing that might change your pay. What would that look like in the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need about half the site to sign up before the company has to talk to us. Right now I've got maybe 90 cards out of 300, mostly nights. I'd do the breaks on days too, sit in the canteen with a stack of forms, and talk to people one by one about the cold-store allowance we never got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the money got really tight, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car goes first; it's an old hatchback that drinks money anyway, and I can get the night bus if I swap to the earlier start. Then Jonas and I stop the takeaway on Fridays. Rent is the one thing we'd never miss, because our landlord has already hinted he could get more for the flat.

say: **Hype or not**, we're still underpaid, and that's what I'd talk about at work.
I'd use the quiet on robots to push the **union drive** harder.
think: My **job is safe** here, but my rent and Jonas's cut hours already squeeze us.
Nothing changing still leaves me with **under a month** of savings and no raise.
do: Get the **union cards** from 90 to about 150 by talking to the day shift.
Put aside **50 a month**, taking the bus some weeks instead of the car.
Keep leading the **night crew** and ignore AI tools completely.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, because the money grind is already there.
S0.quote: Nothing changing isn't the same as things being fine for me.
fieldNote: Even with no AI shock, her **rent rise** and partner's cut hours keep money tense.
She turns every scenario towards **pay and recognition**, not technology.
Proud of her craft: talks about a **square pallet** the way others talk about art.

steps.text: Collect union cards from day-shift pickers at canteen breaks
Set aside 50 a month by taking the night bus some weeks
Keep leading the 14-person night picking crew as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robots are coming slowly, so we've got time to get organised before they arrive. At work I'd be telling everyone to join the union now, not when the first shuttle system goes in. Online I'd share stuff about laws that make companies pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, our site is exactly the kind they'd automate. Head office already flew managers to see a goods-to-person system, where shelves drive to a picker instead of the picker walking. My picking days are counted, maybe not this year, but within five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written promise that nobody is let go without a proper offer of another job or training. I'd ask the regional council about the free forklift-instructor course, since that's the closest thing to a plan I'd accept. And I'd cut the car and start saving properly, 100 a month if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then angry. I hate the idea of learning some screen system I didn't choose, but I hate more the idea of them deciding it all without us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. If the new system meant working with screens and software, would you learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd learn the bit I had to and not a click more. I tried a planning app once for my shifts and gave up after a week. I trust my own head and my headset more than something that guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danuta, she's 54 and the best case-stacker we have, but she reads slowly and hates computers. If the new jobs are all screens and tablets, she's out first. I'd want the union deal to cover people like Danuta, not just the young ones.

say: The robots are **coming slowly**, so this is the time to get organised.
Companies that automate should **pay for retraining**, and I'd share that online.
think: Our site is exactly the kind they'd automate, with a **goods-to-person** system within five years.
I'd rather learn a **forklift-instructor** course than any screen system I'm forced into.
do: Push for a **written promise** of retraining or redeployment before any lay-offs.
Ask the council about the **free instructor course** this year.
Sell the car and save **100 a month**.
feel: **Uneasy**, then angry that the decisions may be made without the workers.
S1.quote: My picking days are counted, maybe not this year, but within five.
fieldNote: She sees the threat in **robots**, not thinking AI, and dates it at about five years.
Resistant to new tech, but will retrain into something **familiar and physical**.
Protective of older crew members like **Danuta**, and frames the fight as collective.

steps.text: Push the union for a written no-lay-off-without-retraining promise
Ask the regional council about the free forklift-instructor course
Sell the old hatchback and save 100 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let a few tech firms run everything with no rules. At work I'd be loud: we need a union deal now, before 2031, not after. Online I'd sign every petition for a pause or a tax on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means in about five years I'm out, and so is nearly everyone I know on the site. The thinking stuff goes first, so the planners and the office lot get hit in 2028, and then by 2031 a robot is picking my yoghurt. I've got no degree, a forklift licence and less than a month saved, so I don't see what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the three years between AGI and the robots to fight for redundancy pay and a retraining fund for every picker. I'd go to the council and the local MP's office with the union and ask for a public jobs plan for the town. And I'd talk to Jonas about moving in with his parents to save rent while we figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly scared. Picturing my crew in the canteen the week the robots arrive makes me feel sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots come around 2031. What would you do with those three years after the thinking AI arrives in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking, because they'd still need us, but I'd treat every month like it was a countdown. I'd be on the union committee pushing for a big redundancy payment and a training fund. Three years sounds long, but on a night shift it goes in a blink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with Jonas's parents. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. His mum would say yes straight away and his dad would make a face, and I'd hate it because I've paid my own way since I was 18. But if it's that or losing the flat, I'd swallow it.

say: Letting tech firms run everything **with no rules** got us here.
Workers need a **union deal** before 2031, and I'd sign every robot-tax petition.
think: By **2031** a robot picks my yoghurt, and nearly everyone I know is out.
With a forklift licence and **under a month** saved, I can't see my next job.
do: Push for **redundancy pay** and a retraining fund through the union committee.
Take a **town jobs plan** to the council and the local MP's office.
Ask Jonas's parents about **moving in** to stop paying rent.
feel: **Properly scared**, picturing her whole crew in the canteen the week robots arrive.
S2.quote: Three years sounds long, but on a night shift it goes in a blink.
fieldNote: She understands the **three-year gap**: office jobs go first, pickers follow by 2031.
Has **no personal plan** beyond collective pressure and moving in with family.
Swallowing her **pride** about family help is the clearest sign of how bad it feels.

steps.text: Push the union committee for redundancy pay and a training fund
Take a public jobs plan to the council and MP's office
Move in with Jonas's parents to stop paying rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them before the companies do. At work I'd keep the union drive at the top of the list. Online I'd share stuff about countries that made firms keep people on while they retrained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the same end for my job, just in 2034 instead of 2031. Eight years feels a bit different, though. I'd be 35, which is still young enough to start again, if anyone paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking and keep leading my crew, because my job is still there for years. I'd get the union to bargain for a training fund now, while the company is still making money and wants peace. I'd also start the forklift-instructor course on my days off, because teaching people is something I'm already good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick than the fast one. It feels like a long tunnel where I can at least see the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The forklift course is still hands-on work, and robots arrive around 2034. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know a robot doesn't need a forklift instructor. But training people for the next thing could still be a job, and I'd rather teach than sit in front of a screen. It buys me a few years, and I need years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Jonas we can't plan a kid or a mortgage until we know where we'll be working. He'd say we never could anyway, and he'd be right. We'd laugh about it and then not sleep.

say: We've got **a few years**, so we should use them before the company does.
Other countries made firms **keep people on** while they retrained, and we can too.
think: My job still ends, just in **2034** instead of 2031.
At **35** I'd be young enough to start again if someone paid for it.
do: Keep picking and **leading the crew** while the job lasts.
Get the union to bargain a **training fund** while the firm is profitable.
Start the **forklift-instructor course** on days off.
feel: **Anxious**, but less sick than the fast picture.
Like a **long tunnel** where she can see the end.
S3.quote: I'd tell my partner Jonas we can't plan a kid or a mortgage until we know where we'll be working.
fieldNote: More time turns **pure alarm** into a slow plan built on teaching.
Knows instructing is **still exposed** to robots, but values the years it buys.
Kids and a **mortgage** are on hold in every version she can picture.

steps.text: Keep leading the night picking crew while the job lasts
Bargain for a company training fund through the union
Start the forklift-instructor course on days off
Put off plans for a child and a mortgage with Jonas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if governments actually bother. At work I'd say the same thing as always: join the union. Online I'd push for the government to plan training now, not in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels different. By 2039 I'd be 40, and I could have a whole second trade by then. The worry is the same people who never did anything for the town before will waste the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking and saving what I can, maybe 100 a month once the car's gone. I'd take the forklift-instructor course and then look at the care sector or teaching adults, because those need people. And I'd stay on the union committee so the plan includes everyone, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer, still worried. I'd sleep, which I wouldn't in the fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the care sector. Is that something you'd really consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nan was in a care home and the staff were run off their feet, so I know it's hard and badly paid. But it's people, not boxes, and I don't think a robot does that well anytime soon. If the pay was fixed, yes, I'd consider it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years to go, does your thin savings still matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It always matters. One broken boiler and we're borrowing from my partner's mum. Ten years doesn't fix that; only better pay does.

say: **Ten years** is enough to do this right, if governments bother.
The government should plan **training now**, not in 2035.
think: By 2039 I'd be 40 with a possible **second trade**.
My real fear is that the people in charge **waste the decade**.
do: Take the **instructor course**, then look into care work or adult teaching.
Save about **100 a month** once the car is sold.
Stay on the **union committee** so the plan covers the whole site.
feel: **Calmer but still worried**; she'd sleep, unlike in the fast pictures.
S4.quote: One broken boiler and we're borrowing from my partner's mum.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her picture a **second career** in care or teaching.
Her **thin cushion** keeps her anxious however much time there is.
Distrust of **local leaders** colours her view of any long plan.

steps.text: Look into care work or adult teaching after the instructor course
Save about 100 a month once the car is sold
Stay on the union committee to shape the site's plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The AGI by 2028 one, no question. Two years for the office lot and five for us pickers is nothing when you've got under a month in the bank. What would help is a law that makes the company pay real redundancy and fund training before a single robot goes in, and a union that's actually recognised so we're at the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. People think warehouse work is nothing. I can build a pallet that won't shift on a mountain road, and if the robots take my job, I want someone to admit that was a skill.

headlineQuote: I can build a pallet that won't shift on a mountain road, and if the robots take my job, I want someone to admit that was a skill.
portrait: Kira, 27, leads a **night picking crew** at a chilled-food warehouse and is proud of her craft.
She has **under a month** saved, rising rent and a partner with cut hours.
She avoids new tech and answers every picture with the **union drive**.
Her mood moves from anxious to **alarmed** in the 2028 picture, and eases slightly with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her picking job could go by 2031 with no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A law forcing **redundancy pay** and funded training before robots arrive.
A **recognised union** so pickers have a seat at the table.
